/-!
# Reshuffling products of finitely supported laws

The sampling procedure of the sub-line lemma produces its six independent
generating blocks in one grouping, while the restricted line-point laws that
the projected marginals must match present the same six blocks in another
grouping.  This module records the rewriting rules that pass between two such
presentations: the support and the weight of a product, the fact that a
push-forward along a bijection is determined by the supports and weights it
compares, and the push-forward of the second factor of a product.

## References

The rewriting rules support `lem:qld-sublines` in
blueprint `lem:qld-sublines`, whose source is
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`.
The product operation is that of blueprint
`def:line-point-dist`.
-/

open scoped BigOperators

namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

open MIPStarRE.LDT

noncomputable section

/-! ## The support and the weight of a product -/

/-- The support of a product law is the product of the supports.  Blueprint
`def:line-point-dist`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:274-287`.
-/
theorem Distribution.prod_support {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq α]
    [DecidableEq β] (μ : Distribution α) (ν : Distribution β) :
    (Distribution.prod μ ν).support = μ.support ×ˢ ν.support := rfl

/-- The weight of a product law is the product of the weights.  Blueprint
`def:line-point-dist`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:274-287`.
-/
theorem Distribution.prod_weight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq α]
    [DecidableEq β] (μ : Distribution α) (ν : Distribution β) (w : α × β) :
    (Distribution.prod μ ν).weight w = μ.weight w.1 * ν.weight w.2 := rfl

/-! ## Push-forward along a bijection -/

/-- A push-forward along a bijection is identified by the supports and the
weights it compares: if the map matches the two supports and carries each
weight to the corresponding weight, and if it has a two-sided inverse, the
push-forward is the target law.  Blueprint
`lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem Distribution.map_bijective_eq {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq α]
    [DecidableEq β] (μ : Distribution α) (ν : Distribution β) (f : α → β)
    (g : β → α) (hgf : ∀ a, g (f a) = a) (hfg : ∀ b, f (g b) = b)
    (hs : ∀ a, a ∈ μ.support ↔ f a ∈ ν.support)
    (hw : ∀ a, μ.weight a = ν.weight (f a)) :
    μ.map f = ν := by
  classical
  refine Distribution.ext_of_support_of_weight ?_ ?_
  · rw [Distribution.map_support]
    ext b
    simp only [Finset.mem_image]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩
      exact (hs a).mp ha
    · intro hb
      refine ⟨g b, (hs (g b)).mpr ?_, hfg b⟩
      rw [hfg b]
      exact hb
  · funext b
    rw [Distribution.map_weight]
    have hfilter : μ.support.filter (fun a => f a = b) =
        μ.support.filter (fun a => a = g b) := by
      ext a
      simp only [Finset.mem_filter]
      constructor
      · rintro ⟨ha, h⟩
        exact ⟨ha, by rw [← h, hgf]⟩
      · rintro ⟨ha, h⟩
        exact ⟨ha, by rw [h, hfg]⟩
    rw [hfilter, Finset.filter_eq' μ.support (g b)]
    by_cases hmem : g b ∈ μ.support
    · rw [if_pos hmem, Finset.sum_singleton, hw (g b), hfg]
    · rw [if_neg hmem, Finset.sum_empty]
      refine (ν.outsideSupport b ?_).symm
      intro hb
      exact hmem ((hs (g b)).mpr (by rw [hfg b]; exact hb))

/-! ## Push-forward of the second factor of a product -/

/-- Pushing the second factor of a product forward is pushing the product
forward along the map acting on that factor alone.  Blueprint
`lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem Distribution.prod_map_right {α β γ : Type*} [DecidableEq α]
    [DecidableEq β] [DecidableEq γ] (μ : Distribution α) (ν : Distribution β)
    (g : β → γ) :
    Distribution.prod μ (ν.map g) =
      (Distribution.prod μ ν).map (fun w => (w.1, g w.2)) := by
  classical
  refine Distribution.ext_of_support_of_weight ?_ ?_
  · change μ.support ×ˢ (ν.support.image g) =
      (μ.support ×ˢ ν.support).image (fun w => (w.1, g w.2))
    ext w
    obtain ⟨x, c⟩ := w
    simp only [Finset.mem_product, Finset.mem_image, Prod.mk.injEq, Prod.exists]
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨hx, b, hb, rfl⟩
      exact ⟨x, b, ⟨hx, hb⟩, rfl, rfl⟩
    · rintro ⟨a, b, ⟨ha, hb⟩, rfl, rfl⟩
      exact ⟨ha, b, hb, rfl⟩
  · funext w
    obtain ⟨x, c⟩ := w
    have hfilter :
        (μ.support ×ˢ ν.support).filter (fun p => (p.1, g p.2) = (x, c)) =
          (μ.support.filter (fun a => a = x)) ×ˢ
            (ν.support.filter (fun b => g b = c)) := by
      ext p
      simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_product, Prod.mk.injEq]
      tauto
    have hx : ∑ a ∈ μ.support.filter (fun a => a = x), μ.weight a =
        μ.weight x := by
      rw [Finset.filter_eq' μ.support x]
      by_cases hmem : x ∈ μ.support
      · rw [if_pos hmem, Finset.sum_singleton]
      · rw [if_neg hmem, Finset.sum_empty, μ.outsideSupport x hmem]
    change μ.weight x * (ν.map g).weight c =
      ∑ p ∈ (μ.support ×ˢ ν.support).filter (fun p => (p.1, g p.2) = (x, c)),
        μ.weight p.1 * ν.weight p.2
    rw [hfilter, Finset.sum_product,
      Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun a _ =>
        (Finset.mul_sum (ν.support.filter (fun b => g b = c))
          (fun b => ν.weight b) (μ.weight a)).symm),
      ← Finset.sum_mul, hx]
    rfl

end

end MIPStarRE.QPBT

/-- The `X` block of the direction of the extended line of a branch lies in

    (kind : LineKind) (k : Fin (2 * P.m + 2))
    (w : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m → DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd) :
    projX (directPointToPauli P (subLineExtDirection P kind k w)) ∈

        ({subLineSourceDirection P kind (subLineXIndex P k)

    cases kind
  · have hval : projZ (directPointToPauli P
        (coordinateDirection (embX P.m i))) = 0 := by
      rw [directPointToPauli_coordinateDirection]
      exact projZ_coordinateDirection_embX i
    change projZ (directPointToPauli P
      (coordinateDirection (embX P.m i))) ∈ _
    rw [hval]
    exact Submodule.zero_mem _
  · rw [subLineZIndex_embX]
    change projZ (directPointToPauli P
      (directPrefixProjection (D := P.extendedDirectLd) (embX P.m i) w)) ∈ _
    rw [projZ_directPrefixProjection_embX]
    change _ ∈ Submodule.span (PauliScalar P)
      ({prefixProjection (P := P.toLdParams) (subLineFirstIndex P)
        (projZ (directPointToPauli P w))} : Set (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))
    rw [prefixProjection_of_val_zero (L := P.toLdParams)
      (i := subLineFirstIndex P) rfl]
    exact Submodule.mem_span_singleton_self _
  · have hval : projZ (directPointToPauli P
        (coordinateDirection (embZ P.m j))) =
        (coordinateDirection j : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P) := by
      rw [directPointToPauli_coordinateDirection]
      exact projZ_coordinateDirection_embZ j
    rw [subLineZIndex_embZ]
    change projZ (directPointToPauli P
      (coordinateDirection (embZ P.m j))) ∈ _
    rw [hval]
    exact Submodule.mem_span_singleton_self _
  · rw [subLineZIndex_embZ]
    change projZ (directPointToPauli P
      (directPrefixProjection (D := P.extendedDirectLd) (embZ P.m j) w)) ∈ _
    rw [projZ_directPrefixProjection_embZ]
    exact Submodule.mem_span_singleton_self _
  · have hval : projZ (directPointToPauli P
        (coordinateDirection (alphaVar P.m))) = 0 := by
      rw [directPointToPauli_coordinateDirection]
      exact projZ_coordinateDirection_alphaVar
    change projZ (directPointToPauli P
      (coordinateDirection (alphaVar P.m))) ∈ _
    rw [hval]
    exact Submodule.zero_mem _
  · change projZ (directPointToPauli P
      (directPrefixProjection (D := P.extendedDirectLd) (alphaVar P.m) w)) ∈ _
    rw [projZ_directPrefixProjection_alphaVar]
    exact Submodule.zero_mem _
  · have hval : projZ (directPointToPauli P
        (coordinateDirection (betaVar P.m))) = 0 := by
      rw [directPointToPauli_coordinateDirection]
      exact projZ_coordinateDirection_betaVar
    change projZ (directPointToPauli P
      (coordinateDirection (betaVar P.m))) ∈ _
    rw [hval]
    exact Submodule.zero_mem _
  · change projZ (directPointToPauli P
      (directPrefixProjection (D := P.extendedDirectLd) (betaVar P.m) w)) ∈ _
    rw [projZ_directPrefixProjection_betaVar]
    exact Submodule.zero_mem _

/-! ## Canonical representatives of the two source blocks -/

/-- Replacing an extended point by its canonical representative in the
direction of the extended line does not change the canonical representative
of its `X` block in the direction of the source `X` line, as soon as the `X`
block of the extended direction lies in the line spanned by the source
direction.  Blueprint `lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem lineRepMap_projX_directPointToPauli_lineRepMap (P : AdmissibleParams)
    (v x : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m → DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd)
    (dX : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
    (hdir : projX (directPointToPauli P v) ∈
      Submodule.span (PauliScalar P) ({dX} : Set (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))) :
    lineRepMap dX (projX (directPointToPauli P (lineRepMap v x))) =
      lineRepMap dX (projX (directPointToPauli P x)) := by
  obtain ⟨t, ht⟩ := Submodule.mem_span_singleton.mp (sub_lineRepMap_mem_span v x)
  obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ := Submodule.mem_span_singleton.mp hdir
  have hx : x = lineRepMap v x + t • v := by
    rw [ht]
    abel
  have hstep : projX (directPointToPauli P x) =
      projX (directPointToPauli P (lineRepMap v x)) +
        (extendedDirectScalarEquiv P t * c) • dX := by
    conv_lhs => rw [hx]
    rw [directPointToPauli_add, directPointToPauli_smul, projX_add, projX_smul,
      ← hc]
    module
  rw [hstep, lineRepMap_add_smul]

/-- Replacing an extended point by its canonical representative in the
direction of the extended line does not change the canonical representative
of its `Z` block in the direction of the source `Z` line, as soon as the `Z`
block of the extended direction lies in the line spanned by the source
direction.  Blueprint `lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem lineRepMap_projZ_directPointToPauli_lineRepMap (P : AdmissibleParams)
    (v x : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m → DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd)
    (dZ : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
    (hdir : projZ (directPointToPauli P v) ∈
      Submodule.span (PauliScalar P) ({dZ} : Set (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P))) :
    lineRepMap dZ (projZ (directPointToPauli P (lineRepMap v x))) =
      lineRepMap dZ (projZ (directPointToPauli P x)) := by
  obtain ⟨t, ht⟩ := Submodule.mem_span_singleton.mp (sub_lineRepMap_mem_span v x)
  obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ := Submodule.mem_span_singleton.mp hdir
  have hx : x = lineRepMap v x + t • v := by
    rw [ht]
    abel
  have hstep : projZ (directPointToPauli P x) =
      projZ (directPointToPauli P (lineRepMap v x)) +
        (extendedDirectScalarEquiv P t * c) • dZ := by
    conv_lhs => rw [hx]
    rw [directPointToPauli_add, directPointToPauli_smul, projZ_add, projZ_smul,
      ← hc]
    module
  rw [hstep, lineRepMap_add_smul]

end

funext j
  have hne : embZ m j ≠ betaVar m := by
    intro h
    simpa using (finCombineEquiv m).symm.injective h
  simp [projZ, coordinateDirection, hne]

/-! ## The coordinates occupied by the two blocks -/

/-- The `i`-th `X`-block coordinate of the extended space is its `i`-th
coordinate.  Blueprint `def:combine-map`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-989`. -/
theorem embX_val (m : ℕ) (i : Fin m) : (embX m i).val = i.val := rfl

/-- The `i`-th `Z`-block coordinate of the extended space is its `(m + i)`-th
coordinate.  Blueprint `def:combine-map`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-989`. -/
theorem embZ_val (m : ℕ) (i : Fin m) : (embZ m i).val = m + i.val := rfl

/-- The extended coordinate carrying the first scalar is the coordinate
`2 m`.  Blueprint `def:combine-map`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-989`. -/
theorem alphaVar_val (m : ℕ) : (alphaVar m).val = 2 * m := by
  simp [alphaVar, finCombineEquiv]

/-- The extended coordinate carrying the second scalar is the coordinate
`2 m + 1`.  Blueprint `def:combine-map`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:970-989`. -/
theorem betaVar_val (m : ℕ) : (betaVar m).val = 2 * m + 1 := by
  simp [betaVar, finCombineEquiv]

/-! ## The blocks of a point of an extended line -/

/-- Transporting the extended scalar field to the source scalar field carries
a point of a line to a point of the transported line, since the transport is
a coordinatewise field isomorphism.  Blueprint
`lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem directPointToPauli_mem_linePoints (P : AdmissibleParams)
    {b d x : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m → DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd}
    (hx : x ∈ linePoints b d) :
    directPointToPauli P x ∈
      linePoints (directPointToPauli P b) (directPointToPauli P d) := by
  obtain ⟨t, rfl⟩ := hx
  refine ⟨extendedDirectScalarEquiv P t, ?_⟩
  funext i
  simp [directPointToPauli]

/-- The `X` block of a point of a line lies on the source line through the
canonical representative of the `X` block of the base, as soon as the `X`
block of the direction is a multiple of the source direction.  Blueprint
`lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem projX_mem_linePoints {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ}
    (b d : Fin (2 * m + 2) → K) (dX : Fin m → K)
    (hd : projX d ∈ Submodule.span K ({dX} : Set (Fin m → K)))
    {x : Fin (2 * m + 2) → K} (hx : x ∈ linePoints b d) :
    projX x ∈ linePoints (lineRepMap dX (projX b)) dX := by
  obtain ⟨t, rfl⟩ := hx
  obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ := Submodule.mem_span_singleton.mp hd
  rw [linePoints_eq_of_mem _ dX (projX b)
    (mem_linePoints_lineRepMap dX (projX b))]
  refine ⟨t * c, ?_⟩
  rw [projX_add, projX_smul, ← hc]
  module

/-- The `Z` block of a point of a line lies on the source line through the
canonical representative of the `Z` block of the base, as soon as the `Z`
block of the direction is a multiple of the source direction.  Blueprint
`lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem projZ_mem_linePoints {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ}
    (b d : Fin (2 * m + 2) → K) (dZ : Fin m → K)
    (hd : projZ d ∈ Submodule.span K ({dZ} : Set (Fin m → K)))
    {x : Fin (2 * m + 2) → K} (hx : x ∈ linePoints b d) :
    projZ x ∈ linePoints (lineRepMap dZ (projZ b)) dZ := by
  obtain ⟨t, rfl⟩ := hx
  obtain ⟨c, hc⟩ := Submodule.mem_span_singleton.mp hd
  rw [linePoints_eq_of_mem _ dZ (projZ b)
    (mem_linePoints_lineRepMap dZ (projZ b))]
  refine ⟨t * c, ?_⟩
  rw [projZ_add, projZ_smul, ← hc]
  module

/-! ## Incidence of the blocks of an extended line -/

/-- The identification of the extended scalar field with the source scalar
field carries an elementary coordinate direction to the elementary coordinate
direction at the same coordinate.  Blueprint
`lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem directPointToPauli_coordinateDirection (P : AdmissibleParams)
    (k : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m) :
    directPointToPauli P (coordinateDirection k) = coordinateDirection k := by
  funext j
  simp [directPointToPauli, coordinateDirection, Pi.single_apply]

/-- Incidence of the `X` blocks: if a source line has as base the canonical
representative, in its own direction, of the `X` block of the base of an
extended line, and if the `X` block of the direction of the extended line
lies in the span of the source direction, then the `X` block of every point
of the extended line is a point of the source line.  Blueprint
`lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem projX_mem_pointSet (P : AdmissibleParams)
    (base dir : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m → DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd)
    (lineX : LineDesc P.toLdParams)
    (hbase : lineX.base =
      lineRepMap lineX.direction (projX (directPointToPauli P base)))
    (hdir : projX (directPointToPauli P dir) ∈
      Submodule.span (PauliScalar P)
        ({lineX.direction} : Set (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)))
    {u : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m → DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd}
    (hu : u ∈ linePoints base dir) :
    projX (directPointToPauli P u) ∈ lineX.pointSet := by
  rw [LineDesc.pointSet, hbase]
  exact projX_mem_linePoints _ _ _ hdir (directPointToPauli_mem_linePoints P hu)

/-- Incidence of the `Z` blocks: if a source line has as base the canonical
representative, in its own direction, of the `Z` block of the base of an
extended line, and if the `Z` block of the direction of the extended line
lies in the span of the source direction, then the `Z` block of every point
of the extended line is a point of the source line.  Blueprint
`lem:qld-sublines`, paper
`references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:1063-1116`. -/
theorem projZ_mem_pointSet (P : AdmissibleParams)
    (base dir : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m → DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd)
    (lineZ : LineDesc P.toLdParams)
    (hbase : lineZ.base =
      lineRepMap lineZ.direction (projZ (directPointToPauli P base)))
    (hdir : projZ (directPointToPauli P dir) ∈
      Submodule.span (PauliScalar P)
        ({lineZ.direction} : Set (Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)))
    {u : Fin P.extendedDirectLd.m → DirectScalarQ P.extendedDirectLd}
    (hu : u ∈ linePoints base dir) :
    projZ (directPointToPauli P u) ∈ lineZ.pointSet := by
  rw [LineDesc.pointSet, hbase]
  exact projZ_mem_linePoints _ _ _ hdir (directPointToPauli_mem_linePoints P hu)

end

end MIPStarRE.QPBT

1	\section{Classical and Quantum Low-degree Tests}
     2	\label{sec:ldt}
     3	
     4	In this section we introduce the classical and quantum low individual degree tests, that form the basis of our classical, quantum-sound and quantum PCP constructions. For quantum soundness of the classical test we refer to~\cite{ML20}. For the quantum test, we refer to~\cite{natarajan2018low} and its adaptation to the low individual degree test given in Appendix~\ref{sec:qld-analysis}. 
     5	The protocol in this work combines both of these tests, using the quantum
     6	low individual degree test for question reduction and the classical low individual degree test for
     7	answer reduction.
     8	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier} below introduces the classical test,
     9	and Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier} does the same for the quantum 
    10	test.
    11	Prior to doing this, we introduce the \emph{Magic Square game} in
    12	Section~\ref{sec:ms}, a key subroutine in the quantum test.
    13	
    14	
    15	\subsection{The classical low-degree test}
    16	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    17	
    18	We begin with a generalization of the classical low-degree test known as the
    19	``simultaneous individual low-degree test''.
    20	We sometimes refer to this as the ``classical low-degree test'' for short.
    21	The low-degree test is used as a subroutine in the Pauli Basis test (see
    22	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) as well as the answer-reduction normal form
    23	verifier (see Section~\ref{sec:ans}).
    24	We describe the test as a nonlocal game in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game} and show
    25	that the question distribution can be implemented as a (typed) conditionally
    26	linear distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL
    27	distributions).
    28	
    29	
    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99	
   100	
   101	
   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}
   175	
   176	
   177	
   178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.
   238

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}

   274	For later convenience we make the following definition. 
   275	
   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
   432	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   433	      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
   434	    \end{split}
   435	  \end{equation*}
   436	  where $\delta_{\ld} = \delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc)$, 
   437	  and all three statements are with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$.
   438	In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
   439		whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
   440	\end{theorem}
   441	
   442	\begin{proof}
   443	Let $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
   444	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
   445	and $m$ divides $q$. Let $\Sigma=\F_q$. Let $\code \subseteq \Sigma^q$ be the Reed-Solomon code with degree $d$. Explicitly, $\code$ is the set of all $(p(x_1),\ldots,p(x_n))$ where $p:\F_q\to\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are an enumeration of $\F_q$. Then in the (standard) notation from~\cite{ji2021quantum} $\code$ is a linear $[q,d+1,n-d+1]_\Sigma$ code.
   446	
   447	Observe that the two-prover tensor code test, for the code $\code^{\otimes m}$, as described in~\cite[Figure 1 and Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}, is identical to the game $\game^\ld$ with parameters $\ldparams$ and $\ldc=1$, whose decider is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}. This is because 
   448	\begin{enumerate}
   449	\item The \emph{axis-parallel line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{axis-parallel lines test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with the only difference that in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} the roles of A and B are chosen uniformly at random. This is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor code test from~\cite[Section 4.1]{ji2021quantum}.
   450	\item The \emph{diagonal line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{subcube commutation test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with again the added symmetrization between players. 
   451	\item The \emph{consistency test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{synchronicity test} from~\cite[Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}.
   452	\end{enumerate}
   453	
   454	As a result,~\cite[Theorem 4.7]{ji2021quantum}, in which we choose the parameter $k$ as $k=m^3d$,  immediately yields \Cref{lem:ld-soundness}.
   455	
   456	To conclude it remains to extend the result to the case of general $\ldc$. This is done 
   457	via a standard reduction, following exactly the same steps as the derivation of Theorem 4.43 from Theorem 4.40 in~\cite{NW19}.
   458	\end{proof}

   465	\subsubsection{Complexity of the classical low-degree test.}
   466	The CL functions and decision procedure of the low-degree test are incorporated
   467	as subroutines in some of the normal form verifiers constructed in subsequent
   468	sections.
   469	The next lemma establishes the time complexity of these procedures as a function
   470	of the parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$.
   471	The lemma also establishes the time complexity of computing the {description} of
   472	the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ as a Turing machine, given the parameter
   473	tuple $\ldparams$ as input.
   474	
   475	
   476	
   477	\begin{lemma}[Complexity of the classical low-degree test]
   478	  \label{lem:ld-complexity}
   479	  Let $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$ denote a parameter tuple.
   480	  \begin{enumerate}
   481		\item The time complexity of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$
   482	    parametrized by $\ldparams$ is $\poly(m, d, k, \log q)$.
   483		\item The time complexity of evaluating marginals of the CL functions
   484	    $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$, and $L_\DLine$ at a given input point is $\poly(m, \log
   485	    q)$.
   486		\item The Turing machine description of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$
   487	    parametrized by $\ldparams$ can be computed from $\ldparams$ in $\polylog
   488	    (q,m,d,k)$ time.
   489	  \end{enumerate}
   490	\end{lemma}
   491	
   492	\begin{proof}
   493		Finite field arithmetic over $\F_q$ can be performed in time $\polylog q$, by
   494	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}.
   495		The most expensive step in $\decider^\ld$ is to evaluate a univariate
   496	  polynomial $f: \F_q \to \F_q^k$ at some point $t_u \in \F_q$ that corresponds
   497	  to a point $u \in \F_q^m$, which takes time $\poly(m,d,k,\log q)$.
   498	  The function $L_\Point$ is a projection onto $V_\xpt$, which takes time
   499	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ to compute (it just involves ``zeroing out'' the registers
   500	  outside of $V_\xpt$).
   501	  The functions $L_\ALine$ and $L_\DLine$ require computing a canonical linear
   502	  map, which requires performing Gaussian elimination and can be done in time
   503	  $\poly(m,\log q)$.
   504	
   505	  The Turing-machine description of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ can be
   506	  uniformly computed from the integers $(q,m,d,k)$ expressed in binary; the
   507	  complexity of computing the description comes from describing the parameter
   508	  tuple $\ldparams$, which takes time that is at most polynomial in the bit
   509	  length of $(q,m,d,k)$.
   510	\end{proof}

   512	\subsection{The Magic Square game}
   513	\label{sec:ms}
   514	
   515	We recall the \emph{Magic Square game} of Mermin and
   516	Peres~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible,aravind2002simple}.
   517	The Magic Square game is a simple self-test for EPR pairs (it tests for two of
   518	them). In addition, it allows one to test that a pair of observables
   519	\emph{anticommutes}.
   520	Here we use it as a building block to construct the quantum low-degree test. 
   521	
   522	There are several formulations of the Magic Square game; here we present it as a
   523	\emph{binary constraint satisfaction} game~\cite{cleve2014characterization}.
   524	In this formulation of the game (denoted by $\game_\MS$) there are $6$ linear
   525	equations defined over $9$ variables that take values in $\F_2$.
   526	The variables correspond to the cells of a $3 \times 3$ grid, as depicted in
   527	Figure~\ref{fig:ms}.
   528	Five of the equations correspond to the constraint that the sum of the variables
   529	in each row and the first two columns must be equal to $0$, and the last
   530	equation requires that the sum of the variables in the last column must be equal
   531	to $1$.

   550	The question set $\type^\ms$ of the Magic Square game is the following:
   551	\begin{equation*}
   552	  \begin{split}
   553	    \type^\msc & = \{ \Constraint_i : i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\}\;,\\
   554	    \type^\msv & = \{ \Variable_j : j = 1, 2, \ldots, 9\}\;,\\
   555	    \type^\ms & = \type^\msc \cup \type^\msv\;.
   556	  \end{split}
   557	\end{equation*}
   558	The questions $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ correspond to the three row
   559	constraints, the questions $\Constraint_4$, $\Constraint_5$ correspond to the first
   560	two column constraints, and question $\Constraint_6$ corresponds to the third
   561	column constraint.
   562	
   563	In the Magic Square game, the verifier first samples a constraint $\Constraint_i
   564	\in \type^\msc$ uniformly at random, and then samples $\Variable_j$, one of the
   565	three variables in the row or column corresponding to $\Constraint_i$, uniformly
   566	at random.
   567	One player is randomly assigned to be the $\Constraint$ player, and the other is
   568	assigned to be the $\Variable$ player.
   569	The $\Constraint$ player is sent the question $\Constraint_i$ and is expected to
   570	respond with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$,
   571	where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables corresponding to
   572	$\Constraint_i$.
   573	The $\Variable$ player is given question $\Variable_j$ and is expected to
   574	respond with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$.
   575	The players win if the $\Constraint$ player's answers satisfy the equation
   576	associated with $\Constraint_i$, and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   577	More precisely, the verifier samples an edge of the type graph (see Section~\ref{sec:types}) $G^\ms$
   578	in Fig.~\ref{fig:type-graph-ms}, sends one endpoint to a random player, and the
   579	other endpoint to the other player.

   612	The following theorem records the self-testing (also known as \emph{rigidity})
   613	properties of the Magic Square game.
   614	Its self-testing properties
   615	are crucial to the Pauli basis test.
   616	In particular, it is used to enforce anticommutation relations between certain
   617	pairs of operators.
   618	We will refer to this theorem in the proof of the soundness of the Pauli basis test (\Cref{thm:pauli} below) in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}.
   619	
   620	\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the Magic Square game]
   621	  \label{thm:ms-rigidity}
   622	
   623	
   624	Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ be a strategy that succeeds in the Magic Square game $\game^{\MS}$ with probability $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ is a state. Then there exist local isometries $\phi_A: \mH_A \to \mH_{A'} \otimes \mH_{A''},\phi_B: \mH_B \to \mH_{B'} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ (where $\mH_{A'},\mH_{B'} \cong (\C^2)^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mH_{A''},\mH_{B''}$ are finite dimensional) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{A''} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ such that 
   625	\begin{enumerate}
   626	    \item $\left \| \phi_A \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2} \otimes \ket{\aux} \right \| \leq O(\sqrt{\eps})$,
   627	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have that
   628	    \begin{gather*}
   629	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^X_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   630	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^Z_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   631	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^X_b)_{B'} \\
   632	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^Z_b)_{B'}
   633	    \end{gather*}
   634	    where the $\approx_{\sqrt{\eps}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}_{A'B'} \otimes \ket{\aux}_{A''B''}$ and the answer summation is over $b \in \{0,1\}$. As a consequence, letting 
   635	    \begin{gather*}
   636	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_1 \\
   637	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_1 \\
   638	    \end{gather*}
   639	    it holds that
   640	    \begin{gather*}
   641	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} \otimes I_{B' B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \otimes I_{B' B''} \\
   642	        I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \;,
   643	      \end{gather*}
   644	      where the notation $M \approx_{\delta} N$ for $M, N$ that are not POVM
   645	      elements means
   646	      \[  \bra{\psi} (M-N)^\dagger (M-N) \ket{\psi}  \leq  O(\delta). \]
   647	\end{enumerate}
   648	
   649	\end{theorem}
   650	\begin{proof}
   651	 	A proof of the rigidity of the Magic Square game can be found in~\cite[Theorem 6.9]{coladangelo2017robust}. There are a couple minor differences between their rigidity statement and the one stated here. First, they state that the robustness of the Magic Square self-test is $O(\eps)$; however they specify the closeness between the actual and ideal states in terms of the trace norm, whereas we specify the closeness between $\phi_\alice \otimes \phi_\bob \ket{\psi}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}\otimes \ket{\aux}$ in terms of the Euclidean distance, which translates to $O(\sqrt{\eps})$ instead of $O(\eps)$. Second, their choice of ideal strategy specifies that the observables corresponding to $\Variable_1$ and $\Variable_5$ questions are $I \otimes \sigma^Z$ and $\sigma^{Z} \sigma^{X} \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$; however under a local change of basis these are equivalent to $\sigma^X \otimes I$ and $\sigma^Z \otimes I$ respectively.
   652	\end{proof}
   653	
   654	We will need the following theorem,
   655	which shows that any pair of anticommuting observables 
   656	can be used to form a value-$1$ strategy for the Magic Square game.
   657	
   658	\begin{theorem}
   659	  \label{thm:ms-from-ac}
   660	  Let $A = \{A_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ and $B = \{B_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ be two-outcome
   661	  projective measurements acting on $(\C^q)^{\otimes n}$ which are consistent on
   662	  $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n}$, and let $\mathcal{O}_A = A_0 - A_1$ and
   663	  $\mathcal{O}_B = B_0 - B_1$ be the corresponding observables.
   664	  Suppose that $\mathcal{O}_A \mathcal{O}_B = -\mathcal{O}_B \mathcal{O}_A$.
   665	  Then there exists a symmetric strategy $\strategy = (\psi, M)$ for the Magic
   666	  Square game with the following properties.
   667	  \begin{enumerate}
   668	  \item $\strategy$ is an SPCC strategy of value $1$.
   669	  \item The state $\ket{\psi}$ has the form $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes
   670	      n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}$.
   671	  \item For $b \in \{0,1\}$, we have $M^{\Variable_1}_b = A_b \otimes I$ and
   672	    $M^{\Variable_5}_b = B_b \otimes I$.\label{item:embeds}
   673	  \end{enumerate}
   674	\end{theorem}
   675	
   676	\begin{proof}
   677	  The strategy~$\strategy$ is based on the canonical two-qubit strategy for the
   678	  Magic Square game as described in, for example,~\cite{aravind2002simple}.
   679	  The state is $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}$.
   680	  We specify the measurements of~$\strategy$ in
   681	  Figure~\ref{fig:ms-operator-soln} as an \emph{operator solution} for the Magic
   682	  Square game, meant to be read as follows: each cell contains a two-outcome
   683	  projective measurement $\{E_0, E_1\}$ on $(\C^q)^{\otimes n} \otimes \C^2$
   684	  written as its \emph{$\pm 1$-valued observable} $E_0 - E_1$.
   685	  When Player~$\alice$ or~$\bob$ receives the question $\Variable_j$ for $j \in
   686	  \{1, \ldots, 9\}$, they measure their share of~$\ket{\psi}$ using the
   687	  measurement specified by the cell corresponding to~$\Variable_j$ and receive a
   688	  single-bit measurement.
   689	  When they receive the question $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,6\}$,
   690	  they simultaneously perform the three measurements in the corresponding row or
   691	  column on $\ket{\psi}$ to obtain three bits.
   692	  For example, if Player~$\alice$ receives question~$\Variable_1$, they
   693	  measure~$\ket{\psi}$ using the measurement $\{A_0 \otimes I, A_1 \otimes I\}$
   694	  corresponding to the observable $\cal{O}_A \otimes I$ (where the first
   695	  operator acts on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n}$ and the second acts on
   696	  $\ket{\EPR_2}$).
   697	  Similarly, on question~$\Variable_5$, they use the measurement $\{B_0 \otimes
   698	  I, B_1 \otimes I\}$.
   699	  This establishes Item~\ref{item:embeds} of the theorem.

   723	  First, we show that this gives a well-defined strategy.
   724	  The $\Variable_j$ measurements are well-defined because each cell contains a
   725	  $\pm 1$-valued observable.
   726	  This is obvious for all $j \neq 9$; when $j = 9$, the bottom-right cell
   727	  contains $\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$.
   728	  Because~$\cal{O}_A$ and~$\cal{O}_B$ anti-commute,
   729	  \begin{equation}\label{eq:am-i-hermitian}
   730	  \cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X
   731	  = - \cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X \sigma^Z
   732	  = \cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^X \sigma^Z
   733	  = (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)^\dagger.
   734	  \end{equation}
   735	  As a result, this matrix is Hermitian. In addition, 
   736	  \begin{equation*}
   737	  (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)^2
   738	  = (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X) \cdot (\cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^X \sigma^Z)
   739	  = (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \cdot \cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A) \otimes (\sigma^Z \sigma^X \cdot \sigma^X \sigma^Z)
   740	  = I,
   741	  \end{equation*}
   742	  where the first step uses Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian} and the final
   743	  step uses the fact that $\cal{O}_A, \cal{O}_B, \sigma^X, \sigma^Z$ are $\pm
   744	  1$-valued observables and hence square to the identity.
   745	  As a result, this matrix is Hermitian and squares to the identity.
   746	  Therefore, it is a $\pm 1$-valued observable.
   747	  
   748	  As for the $\Constraint_i$ measurements,
   749	  we must show that the three measurements in each row and column are simultaneously measurable.
   750	  This is equivalent to the three $\pm 1$-valued observables being simultaneously diagonalizable,
   751	  which is equivalent to them being pairwise commuting. This can be easily verified for the cases of $i = 1, 2, 4, 5$
   752	  (i.e.\ the first two rows and columns).
   753	  In the case of $i = 3$, commutativity of $\cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^Z$ and $\cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X$ 
   754	  follows from Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian}.
   755	  Since these two matrices commute, they also commute with their product 
   756	  $(\cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^Z)(\cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X) = \cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$.
   757	  The case of $i = 6$ is similar.
   758	  
   759	  By construction, $\strategy$ is symmetric, and we have already shown that it
   760	  is projective.
   761	  It remains to show that it is commuting, consistent, and value~$1$.
   762	  To show that it is commuting, it suffices to show that the measurement for
   763	  each cell is simultaneously measurable with all three measurements in its row
   764	  or column, which was already proved above.
   765	  Now we show consistency of the measurements.
   766	  We will show this by instead showing consistency of their observables.
   767	  By this we mean the following: if $E = \{E_0, E_1\}$ is a two-outcome projective measurement on $\cal{H}$
   768	  then its corresponding $\pm 1$-valued observable $\cal{O} = E_0 - E_1$
   769	  is consistent on a state $\ket{\phi} \in \cal{H} \otimes \cal{H}$ if
   770	  \begin{equation*}
   771	  \cal{O}\otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi} = I_{\alice} \otimes \cal{O} \cdot \ket{\phi}.
   772	  \end{equation*}
   773	  This is in fact equivalent to the notion of $E$ being consistent on $\ket{\phi}$ from Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement}.
   774	  To see this, if $E$ is consistent on $\ket{\phi}$, then so is $\cal{O}$, because
   775	  \begin{equation*}
   776	  \cal{O}\otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   777	  = (E_0 - E_1) \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   778	  = I_{\alice} \otimes (E_0 - E_1) \cdot \ket{\phi}
   779	  = I_{\alice} \otimes \cal{O} \cdot \ket{\phi},
   780	  \end{equation*}
   781	  where the second equality is by consistency of~$E$.
   782	  On the other hand, suppose $\cal{O}$ is consistent on $\ket{\phi}$.
   783	  Then because $E_0 + E_1 = I$, we can write $E_0 = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I + \cal{O})$ and $E_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I - \cal{O})$.
   784	  As a result,
   785	  \begin{equation*}
   786	  E_0 \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   787	  = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I + \cal{O}) \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   788	  = I_{\alice} \otimes \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I + \cal{O}) \cdot \ket{\phi}
   789	  = I_{\alice} \otimes E_0 \cdot \ket{\phi},
   790	  \end{equation*}
   791	  and similarly for $E_0$. Thus, $E$ is consistent on $\ket{\phi}$.
   792	  This proves the equivalence.
   793	  
   794	  Now we use this to prove consistency of $\strategy$.
   795	  To begin, we note that because $A$ and $B$ are consistent on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n}$ by assumption,
   796	  so to are their $\pm 1$-valued observables $\cal{O}_A$ and $\cal{O}_B$.
   797	  Next, we note that $\sigma^X$ and $\sigma^Z$ are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$;
   798	  to verify this, we recall that $\sigma^X \ket{0} = \ket{1}$ and $\sigma^X \ket{1} = \ket{0}$, and so
   799	  \begin{align*}
   800	  \sigma^X \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}
   801	&  =   \sigma^X \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\ket{00} + \ket{11})\\
   802	&  = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\ket{10} + \ket{01})
   803	    =    I_{\alice} \otimes \sigma^X \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\ket{11} + \ket{00})
   804	    =    I_{\alice} \otimes \sigma^X \cdot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}.
   805	  \end{align*}
   806	  This shows $\sigma^X$ is consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$,
   807	  and a similar argument shows the same for $\sigma^Z$.
   808	  We now use these two facts to show that the observable in each cell of
   809	  Figure~\ref{fig:ms-operator-soln} is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$.
   810	  To see why, consider the $j = 9$ case:
   811	  \begin{align*}
   812	&  (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)_\alice \otimes I_\bob
   813			\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2} \\
   814	  ={}& (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z)_\alice \otimes (I \otimes \sigma^X)_\bob
   815	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\sigma^X$}\\
   816	  ={}& (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes I)_\alice \otimes (I \otimes \sigma^X\sigma^Z)_\bob
   817	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\sigma^Z$}\\
   818	  ={}& (\cal{O}_A \otimes I)_\alice \otimes ( \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X\sigma^Z)_\bob
   819	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\cal{O}_B$}\\
   820	  ={}& I_\alice \otimes (\cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^X\sigma^Z)_\bob
   821	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\cal{O}_A$}\\
   822	  ={}& I_\alice \otimes (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)_\bob
   823	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}. \tag{by Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian}}
   824	  \end{align*}
   825	  The remaining cases of $j \in\{1, \ldots, 8\}$ are similar, and we omit them.
   826	  This shows that the observable in each cell is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$,
   827	  and as a result the corresponding two-outcome projective measurements are consistent as well.
   828	  As a result, the $\Variable_j$ measurements are consistent.
   829	  
   830	  As for the $\Constraint_i$ measurements, each such measurement $\{F_{a, b,
   831	    c}\}_{a, b, c \in \{0, 1\}}$ is of the form $F_{a, b, c} = E^1_a \cdot E^2_b
   832	  \cdot E^3_c$, where $E^1$, $E^2$, and $E^3$ are $\Variable$ measurements.
   833	  But then consistency of~$F$ follows from the~$\Variable$ consistencies:
   834	  \begin{align*}
   835	  F_{a, b, c} \otimes I_{\bob} \ket{\psi}
   836	 & = (E^1_a \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^3_c)_{\alice} \otimes I_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\\
   837	 & = (E^1_a \cdot E^2_b)_{\alice} \otimes (E^3_c)_{\bob} \ket{\psi} \tag{consistency of $E^3$}\\
   838	 &   = (E^1_a)_{\alice} \otimes (E^3_c \cdot E^2_b)_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\tag{consistency of $E^2$}\\
   839	 &       = I_{\alice} \otimes (E^3_c \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^1_a)_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\tag{consistency of $E^1$}\\
   840	 &       = I_{\alice} \otimes (E^1_a \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^2_c)_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\tag{commutativity of $E^1$, $E^2$, and $E^3$}\\
   841	 &               = I_{\alice} \otimes F_{a, b,c} \ket{\psi}.
   842	  \end{align*}
   843	  Hence, all measurements are consistent.
   844	  
   845	  Since all measurements are consistent, this implies that the answer bit of the
   846	  player receiving a $\Variable$ question is always consistent with the
   847	  corresponding answer bit of the player receiving the $\Constraint$ question.
   848	  Similarly, the answers of the player receiving the $\Constraint$ question
   849	  always satisfy the given constraint; observe that in all rows and the first
   850	  two columns, the observables multiply to $I$, whereas the observables in the
   851	  last column multiply to $-I$.
   852	  This implies that the strategy is value-$1$.
   853	  To see why, 
   854	  let us again consider a $\Constraint_i$ measurement, which we write as $F=\{F_{a, b, c}\}_{a, b, c \in \{0, 1\}}$.
   855	  As above, it can be written as  $F_{a, b, c} = E^1_a \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^3_c$, where $E^1$, $E^2$, and $E^3$ are $\Variable$ measurements.
   856	  Consider the measurement $S=\{S_0, S_1\}$ that corresponds to measuring $\{F_{a, b, c}\}$ and then outputting the sum of measured values of~$a$, $b$, and~$c$.
   857	  In other words,
   858	  \begin{equation*}
   859	  S_0 = F_{0, 0, 0} + F_{0, 1, 1} + F_{1, 0, 1} + F_{1, 1, 0},
   860	  \qquad
   861	  S_1 = F_{0, 0, 1} + F_{0, 1, 0} + F_{1, 0, 0} + F_{1, 1, 1}.
   862	  \end{equation*}
   863	  The following expression gives a convenient formula for the $\pm 1$-valued observable $S_0 - S_1$:
   864	  \begin{equation*}
   865	  (E_0^1 - E_1^1) \cdot (E_0^2 - E_1^2) \cdot (E_0^3 - E_1^3)
   866	  = E_0^1 E_0^2 E_0^3 - E_0^1 E_0^2 E_1^3 - E_0^1 E_1^2 E_0^3 + E_0^1 E_1^2 E_1^3 + \cdots
   867	  = S_0 - S_1.
   868	  \end{equation*}
   869	  When we are looking at $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$,
   870	  the left-hand side of this equation is equal to $I$, and so $I = S_0- S_1$.
   871	  Because $S_0$ and $S_1$ are both positive semidefinite,
   872	  this is true only if $S_0 = I$ and $S_1 = 0$, which implies that the three bits output by $F$ always sum to~$0$.
   873	  As a result, this strategy always satisfies the $\Constraint_i$ question.
   874	  On the other hand, when $i = 6$, then the left-hand side of this equation is equal to $-I$,
   875	  and so $S_1 = I$, and the three bits sum to~$1$.
   876	  Thus, the strategy always satisfies the $\Constraint_6$ question as well.
   877	  This concludes the proof.
   878	\end{proof}

   880	\subsection{The Pauli basis test}
   881	\label{sec:pauli-verifier}
   882	
   883	We introduce the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{natarajan2018low} in the form
   884	of a slight modification to it by~\cite{NW19} known as the \emph{Pauli basis
   885	  test}.
   886	Informally, the quantum low-degree test asks the players to measure a large
   887	number of qubits and return a highly compressed version of the measurement
   888	outcome.
   889	The Pauli basis test simply asks that the players return their uncompressed
   890	measurement outcomes, and it is designed by direct reduction to the quantum
   891	low-degree test.
   892	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-game} we describe the Pauli basis test as a nonlocal
   893	game $\game^\pauli$ and show that its question distribution is implementable via
   894	a CL distribution, as we did with the classical low-degree test in
   895	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   896	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-complexity} we exhibit canonical parameters for the
   897	Pauli basis test and give bounds on the time complexity of executing the test.
   898	
   899	\subsubsection{The game}
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}

   971	  \cup \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair\}\;,
   972	\end{equation}
   973	where $\type^\ms$ is the question type set of the Magic Square game defined in
   974	Section~\ref{sec:ms}.

  1073	\paragraph{Conditional linear functions for the Pauli basis test.}
  1074	The CL functions corresponding to the Pauli basis test question distribution are
  1075	parameterized by the parameter tuple $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$.
  1076	Let $V^\pauli$ denote the linear space $(\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m
  1077	\times (\F_q)^2$.
  1078	The space $V^\pauli$ is decomposed into a direct sum of the following register
  1079	subspaces: $V_\xpt,V_\zpt$ (which are $m$-dimensional), $V_\coord$ (which is
  1080	$1$-dimensional), $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is $m$-dimensional), and
  1081	$V_{\rxpt},V_{\rzpt}$ (which are $1$-dimensional).
  1082	We identify elements of $V^\pauli$ as tuples $(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1083	\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m \times (\F_q)^2$.
  1084	We define CL functions $L_\tvar: V^\pauli \to V^\pauli$ for every type $\tvar
  1085	\in \type^\pauli$:
  1086	\begin{enumerate}
  1087	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Point,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1088	  = L_\Point(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\Point$ is the $1$-level CL function defined in
  1089	  \Cref{eq:cl-ptf}.\footnote{The range $V_{\xpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus
  1090	    V_{\dir{}}$ or $V_{\zpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ of $L_\Point$ is
  1091	    embedded in $V^\pauli$ in the natural way.
  1092	    The same convention is used also in Item 2 and 3 for $L_\ALine$ and
  1093	    $L_\DLine$.}
  1094	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\ALine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1095	  = L_\ALine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\ALine$ is the $2$-level CL function defined in
  1096	  \Cref{eq:cl-alnf}.
  1097	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\DLine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1098	  = L_\DLine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\DLine$ is the $3$-level CL function defined in
  1099	  \Cref{eq:cl-dlnf}.
  1100	\item For $\tvar \in \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair, (\Pair,X), (\Pair,Z) \}$,
  1101	  $L_{\tvar}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) =
  1102	  (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,0,0,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, i.e., it projects onto $V_\xpt \oplus
  1103	  V_\zpt \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$.
  1104	  Thus $L_{\tvar}$ is a $1$-level CL function.
  1105	  
  1106	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Pauli,W} = 0$ as the identically $0$
  1107	  function.
  1108	  Thus it is a $0$-level CL function.
  1109	
  1110	\end{enumerate}
  1111	We note that the maps $L_{\Point,W}, L_{\ALine,W}, L_{\DLine,W}$ act as the zero function
  1112	on $V_{\overline{W}} \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$ where $\overline{W} = X$
  1113	if $W = Z$ and $\overline{W} = Z$ if $W = X$.
  1114	
  1115	The question distribution of $\game^\pauli$ is thus a typed CL distribution on
  1116	$\type^\pauli \times V^\pauli \times \type^\pauli \times V^\pauli$ where
  1117	$(\tvar_\alice,x_\alice,\tvar_\bob,x_\bob)$ is sampled by first uniformly
  1118	sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice,\tvar_\bob)$ from the graph $G^\pauli$ defined
  1119	in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli}, sampling a uniformly random $z \in
  1120	V^\pauli$, and then setting $x_w = L_{\tvar_w}(z)$ for $w \in \AB$.
